qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture five. Partitioning. This is how data that is too big for one node gets split across many.
There are twelve orders, but each node has room for only eight.
12 orders; room for eight per node.
So a full copy on every node does not fit.
A full copy per node does not fit.
Instead we split the data, and each order lives in exactly one partition.
Split: each order lives in one partition.
Each partition is also copied to another node, in case one fails.
Each partition is also copied to another node.
With key ranges, each node owns a range of the keys.
Each node owns a range of keys.
Okafor falls between N and S, so node three takes it.
Okafor falls in N to S, so node 3 takes it.
A query from Khan to Mills finds every name on one node.
Khan to Mills: one node holds them all.
That is the benefit. Neighbouring keys sit together.
Neighbouring keys sit together.
Now the key is the time of the write. Each node owns some hours.
Key by time: each node owns hours.
It is the afternoon, so writes go to the node for twelve to seventeen.
It is afternoon: writes go to 12 to 17.
Write after write, they all land on the same node.
Write after write, all on the same node.
That is one hot spot, while three nodes sit idle.
One hot spot while three nodes sit idle.
A hash function turns a key into a number.
A hash turns a key into a number.
Each node owns a range of hash values.
Each node owns a range of hash values.
Keys arrive in order, but land all over the nodes.
Keys arrive in order but land all over.
Eight keys, and every node ends up with two.
Eight keys: two on every node.
Here are the same sixteen users, laid out two ways.
The same 16 users, laid out two ways.
Now ask for ids one hundred and one to one hundred and four.
Now ask for ids 101 to 104.
With key ranges, all four are on one node.
Key ranges: all four are on one node.
With hashing, they are on four different nodes. So range queries get expensive.
Hash: they are on four different nodes.
Each partition indexes only its own cars. This is a local index.
Each partition indexes only its own cars.
Now search for red cars.
Search for red cars.
Any partition may hold one, so we must ask all three.
Any partition may hold one, so ask all three.
Then we gather the answers into one list.
Gather the answers into one list.
The other way is to split the index itself, by term.
Or split the index itself, by term.
Now a search for red reads just one index partition.
A search reads just one index partition.
But saving a blue mini updates two index partitions.
Save a blue mini: two index partitions change.
So reads are cheap, and writes cost more.
Cheap reads, dearer writes.
Twelve items sit on three nodes, and a fourth node joins.
Twelve items on three nodes. A fourth joins.
With hash modulo N, the N changes, so nine of the twelve keys move.
Hash mod N: N changed, so 9 of 12 keys move.
With fixed partitions, the new node steals three whole partitions.
Fixed partitions: it steals 3 whole ones.
Three moves, instead of nine.
Three moves instead of nine.
Each partition has a size limit, here ten gigabytes.
Each partition has a size limit: 10 GB.
As data grows, partition two reaches twelve gigabytes, over the limit.
Data grows: P2 hits 12 GB, over the limit.
So it splits in two, and one half can move to another node.
It splits; one half can move node.
If data shrinks, small neighbours merge.
Data shrinks: neighbours merge.
Split big data into partitions, so that each node holds only a piece.
Key ranges keep keys in order. Hashes spread the load evenly.
When a new node joins, move whole partitions only.
